1.pericope_label: O give thanks unto the Lord, for he is good: Israel, the house of Aaron, and all that fear him

schools.summary: Augustine reduces the three summoned groups to those that fear the Lord, the little and the great, and dwells on the brevity of the reason given for praise, since nothing could be said in fewer words than that God is good.

Calvin reads the psalm as David at his accession, appointed rather than self-made king, and as figuring under a temporal kingdom the eternal kingdom of the Son; Gill denies the literal restriction of all three groups and extends each to the whole people of God.

Henry holds the thanksgiving of all who fear the Lord as pleasing as that of either house, and notes that many who are lifted up will not hear of their former depressions while this psalmist takes every occasion to remember his low estate; Spurgeon urges praise for what God is rather than for what he gives.

Clarke prefers David as author while acknowledging the post-exilic view, reads the house of Aaron as evidence of a restored temple worship, and rejects two elaborate dramatic schemes for the psalm as too mechanical.
Keil and Delitzsch pronounce the psalm without doubt post-exilic, name three possible occasions after the Return, and record the place it held in the affections of a great reformer.

debates: When was the psalm written, and by whom? Calvin reads it as David at his accession and Clarke thinks David most probably the author while acknowledging that many place it after the captivity; Keil and Delitzsch call it without any doubt a post-exilic song and name three occasions after the Return that might have produced it; and a later hand within the Calvin text observes that the psalm has no title at all, canvassing the return from captivity, an anointing at Hebron, the reign of Hezekiah and the age of the Maccabees, with one authority declining to decide.

Is the psalm a dialogue with assigned parts? Clarke reports one scheme that joins it to the psalm before and gives its long middle section to the Messiah, and another that makes the whole a processional song at the temple gate with verses parcelled among a conqueror, his train and the priests within, the temple taken as a type of heaven; he judges both too mechanical and keeps his own simple division.
outliers: The Calvin text carries a later editorial hand which canvasses four datings of the psalm and quotes three nineteenth-century authorities, one of whom declines to decide among them.

Keil and Delitzsch record that this psalm was the favourite of a great reformer, who called it his noblest jewel, his defence and his treasure, said it had helped him out of troubles from which neither emperor nor king could have helped him, and expounded it in the solitude of his exile.
themes: thanks urged on every rank of worshipper
goodness praised for itself and not for its gifts
mercy that endures for ever
a psalm read in procession
the question of who speaks

5.pericope_label: I called upon the Lord in distress: the answer that set him in a large place, and the better trust

schools.summary: Spurgeon notes that the man had prayed before the distress and so prayed easily in it, reports the reading that makes the strait a narrow gorge, and holds that with God hearing means answering.
Gill names four occasions for the distress and makes God the principal helper who stands in the room of all others, and takes the closing verses as the conclusion drawn from the whole experience.

Clarke makes the speaker a living witness who bids others take encouragement, renders the Lord as among his helpers so that he can face his enemies, and judges men of high estate proud and unable or unwilling to deliver.

Ellicott treats two of these verses as reminiscences of earlier psalms, renders the opening as a cry out of straitness answered with freedom, and takes the contrast at the close as one between covenant fidelity and foreign alliance.

debates: Are these verses the psalmist own or assembled from earlier psalms? Ellicott calls one verse a reminiscence of an earlier psalm and another made up of a second, and refers the reader to his notes there; Gill, Clarke and Spurgeon all expound them as immediate personal experience, Gill naming particular occasions for the distress, Clarke making the speaker a living witness of mercy, and Spurgeon observing that he had prayed before the trouble came.

What is the better trust set against? Ellicott takes the contrast politically, as covenant fidelity set against alliance with foreign princes, while allowing the larger application; Clarke reads it as a judgment on the character of the great, who are proud and rash and often cannot deliver and will not when they can; Gill takes it simply as the conclusion of the whole argument.
outliers: Ellicott renders the opening as a cry out of straitness answered with freedom, and sets beside it a line from a play in which a soul is said at last to have elbow-room.
Spurgeon observes that the man had called upon the Lord when he was not in distress, and therefore found it natural and easy to call upon him when he was.
themes: prayer offered out of anguish
a strait exchanged for a large place
God counted among the helpers
trust weighed against human power
experience offered as encouragement

10.pericope_label: All nations compassed me about: the bees, the fire of thorns, and the enemy who thrust sore

schools.summary: Gill expounds the bees from natural history and extends the nations from the psalmist own enemies to those gathered against Christ and to the last battles of prophecy, and takes the sudden singular as an apostrophe to one particular adversary.

Clarke finds two of the finest images of Homer in this passage and quotes both in an English version, and sets out five renderings of the disputed verb from four scholars and three versions; Wesley keeps the nations to the neighbouring peoples and takes the singular enemy collectively.

Ellicott suspects the text of the bees and proposes that a word for comb dropped out through the copyist memory of a passage in the law, explains the point of the fire of thorns from its rapidity, and calls the sudden change of person in the thirteenth verse very dramatic.

debates: What does the comparison with bees mean, and is the text sound? Ellicott holds that the image may be derived from a passage in the law but that the old Greek points to a more expressive original in which the bees surround the comb, the word for comb having possibly dropped out because the copyist was thinking of that passage; Clarke reads the figure as one of the finest images in Homer and quotes the swarms darkening the coast; Gill expounds it from natural history, that bees will attack and kill horses and that besieged places have been relieved by throwing hives among the besiegers.

Is the enemy of the thirteenth verse one or many? Gill takes the singular as an apostrophe to one particular adversary and names three; Ellicott renders that thou didst thrust and thrust at me and calls the change of person and the direct challenge very dramatic; Wesley holds that the singular word is put collectively for all his enemies.
outliers: Ellicott explains a suspected loss in the text psychologically, supposing that the word for comb dropped out because the copyist mind was running on a passage in the law where bees also appear.

Clarke gathers five renderings of one verb from four scholars and three versions, that the psalmist will disappoint them, cut them to pieces, has repelled them, will cut them off, or is avenged on them.
themes: enemies numerous as a swarm
a fire that burns out as fast as it kindles
a name invoked against numbers
one adversary or many
victory ascribed wholly to God

15.pericope_label: The voice of rejoicing in the tabernacles of the righteous: I shall not die but live, and the gates of righteousness

schools.summary: Henry makes the gates a matter of humble suit and the business within them praise, and calls what follows an illustrious prophecy applied by an apostle without contradiction; Spurgeon compares the temple entrance to a famous seat of empire and calls it the true gate of righteousness.

Gill denies that the gate is the door of the sanctuary and makes it the Messiah himself, takes the claim of life as personal and then christological, and distinguishes fatherly chastening from a punishment laid on a surety.

Clarke keeps the scene dramatic, taking one verse for the answer of the Levites to the king, and reduces the claim of life to a man preserved to publish the works of the Lord; Wesley gives the gates a farther prospect than the psalmist, in an ascension and a blessed temple.

Ellicott insists on the literal temple gate and a procession summoning it to open, makes the claim of life the claim of Israel rather than of an individual, ties the sense of the tabernacles to the disputed date, and reads the exalted right hand as a warrior arm lifted to strike.

debates: Are the gates of righteousness the temple doors or something more? Ellicott holds that the next verse explains them as the gate of the temple and that there is not the least reason for taking the words in any but that literal sense, though they admit endless spiritual applications; Gill denies it outright and makes the gate the Messiah himself; Wesley gives the place a farther prospect in an ascension; Henry reports the same reading and draws practical use from it; Clarke keeps the verse dramatic as the answer of the Levites.

Who says that he shall not die but live? Ellicott holds it is Israel and not an individual who claims continuance of life for the display of God glory, while granting that the hope suits each member too; Gill takes it personally, since the psalmist knew he must die and means that these afflictions would not end in death, and then refers the words to Christ; Clarke reads a man preserved to publish the works of the Lord.
outliers: Ellicott observes that whether the tabernacles of the righteous are an actual encampment or tents put poetically for dwellings depends entirely on the view taken of the date and occasion of the psalm, so that the dating question returns inside a single word.
Spurgeon compares the entrance of the temple with a famous eastern title in which a gate stands for a seat of empire, and calls that entrance the true seat of empire and the gate of righteousness.
themes: rejoicing heard in every dwelling
a right hand raised in glory or in war
life claimed for the sake of praise
chastening that stops short of death
admission sought at the gates

22.pericope_label: The stone which the builders refused: the Lord doing, and the day which he hath made

schools.summary: Spurgeon reads the stone first of a king raised into office and then of Christ, and explains the rejection by saying he could not be made to fit the builders ideal of a national church, being of another quarry than themselves.
Gill identifies the stone by rejecting three older readings in turn, and multiplies the possible senses of the day from the entry into the city to the whole gospel dispensation.

Clarke declines to expound the passage and refers the reader to his notes on the gospel, and keeps the day to the occasion of the triumph; Wesley keeps both halves of the figure, the people as stones and the princes as builders, and holds the words agree more properly to Christ than to David.

Ellicott notes the absence of the article and reads a stone rather than the stone, identifies it with Israel counted of no account in the politics of the great powers, and offers the festival or the day of triumph for the day.

debates: Who is the stone the builders refused? Ellicott notes that there is no article and identifies the stone with Israel, of no account in the plans of those shaping the destinies of the eastern nations yet destined by God for a chief place; Gill reaches the opposite conclusion by rejecting in turn the readings that make it a governor of the return, the people of Israel, and the psalmist himself; Wesley and Spurgeon read it first of the king and then, more properly, of Christ.

What is the day which the Lord hath made? Ellicott offers either the festival for which the psalm was composed or the day of the triumph won; Clarke keeps it to the occasion in hand, a gracious opportunity to be improved; Wesley makes it a season sanctified never to be forgotten; Gill offers the entry into the city, the resurrection, the day commemorating it, or the whole gospel dispensation.
outliers: Ellicott gives the rejected stone a political sense, as a people counted of no account by those who were trying to shape the destinies of the eastern nations at their own pleasure.

Spurgeon explains why the builders rejected the stone, that they could see no excellence in him to build upon, that he could not be made to fit their ideal of a national church, and that he was a stone of another quarry than themselves.
themes: a stone rejected and set at the corner
a reversal ascribed wholly to God
a day marked out for rejoicing
the figure applied beyond its first subject
builders who could not use what they had

25.pericope_label: Save now, I beseech thee: the welcome at the gate, the light shown, and the sacrifice bound to the horns

schools.summary: Spurgeon turns the doubled confession into a resolve that as long as he has any being it shall be spent in praise, and observes that the psalm ends as it began, making a complete circle of adoration.

Gill traces the opening cry from a wish of health to a king to its use at the entry into the city, keeps the welcome to the multitude who used it, and reads the light of the coming of the Messiah and of the gospel shining into the heart.

Clarke connects the cry with the branches carried at the feast, reports both the sacrificial and the leafy rendering of the hardest clause, and suggests that a divine splendour may actually have shone upon the procession; Wesley assigns the parts to Levites and priests and takes the horns of the altar as made for binding the victims.

Ellicott corrects the opening words to save, we pray, supplies the rabbinical custom of welcoming pilgrim caravans with the words of the welcome, weighs the literal and figurative senses of the light, and denies that the closing clause can mean tying a victim to the horns.

debates: What light was shown? Ellicott finds the choice difficult, offering a repetition of the earlier verse, or a connection with the pillar of cloud and fire which the feast very probably commemorated, or figuratively the light of salvation, or an allusion to the priestly benediction where the same verb stands; Clarke goes furthest toward the literal and suggests a divine splendour may have shone upon the procession as a proof of approbation; Gill reads the coming of the Messiah and the gospel; Wesley reads dark clouds scattered.

What is bound at the horns of the altar? Clarke reports a paraphrase that binds a victim with chains until it is sacrificed and its blood sprinkled, and a rival rendering that keeps the festival with thick boughs up to the horns, which the old Latin and Greek followed; Wesley takes the plain sacrificial sense and supposes the horns made for that use; Ellicott denies that the plain sense will work, since the Hebrew says as far as to rather than to.
outliers: Ellicott supplies from rabbinical writings the custom by which pilgrim caravans were welcomed on their arrival at the city with the very words of the twenty-sixth verse, spoken by the Levite in charge.
Clarke suggests that at this point in the procession a divine splendour perhaps shone upon the whole company, as a proof of God approbation.
themes: a cry for salvation become a greeting
a welcome spoken from the gate
light literal or figurative
a festival victim or a leafy bough
a psalm closing where it began
